paragraphs: Liberty is not the fruit of every climate, so it is not within reach of every people. The more one considers this principle, laid down by Montesquieu, the truer it seems; the more it is attacked, the more chances it gets to be confirmed by new proofs.

In every government that exists, the public person consumes without producing. Where, then, does it get what it consumes? From the labor of its members. The needs of the public are supplied out of the surplus of individuals. It follows that the civil State can survive only as long as people’s labor yields them more than they need.

The amount of this surplus is not the same in all countries. In some it is considerable, in others middling, in others nothing, and in some even negative. The relation of product to subsistence depends on the fertility of the climate, on the kind of labor the land demands, on the nature of its products, on the strength of its inhabitants, on how much or how little they find necessary to consume, and on several further considerations that together make up the whole relation.

On the other hand, not all governments are of the same nature: some are more voracious than others, and the differences between them rest on this second principle, that the farther public contributions travel from their source, the more burdensome they become.

The burden should be measured not by the amount of the taxes but by the path they must travel to get back to those they came from. When the circulation is quick and well established, it does not matter whether the people pay much or little; the people are always rich and, financially speaking, all is well. But if what the people pay does not return to them, however little it is, they are soon exhausted by giving continually. The State is then never rich, and the people are always a people of beggars.

It follows that the greater the distance between people and government, the more burdensome taxation becomes. So in a democracy the people bear the lightest burden; in an aristocracy, a heavier one; and in a monarchy the weight is heaviest. Monarchy therefore suits only wealthy nations; aristocracy, States of middling size and wealth; and democracy, States that are small and poor.

In fact, the more we reflect, the more we find that the difference between free States and monarchical ones is this: in the former, everything is used for the public advantage; in the latter, the public forces and those of individuals affect each other, and each grows as the other weakens. Finally, instead of governing subjects to make them happy, despotism makes them wretched in order to govern them.
We find, then, in every climate, natural causes from which we can determine the form of government that the climate requires, and we can even say what kind of inhabitants it should have.

Unfriendly and barren lands, where the product does not repay the labor, should remain desert and uncultivated, or be peopled only by savages. Lands where people’s labor yields no more than the bare _minimum_ needed to live should be inhabited by barbarous peoples; in such places no polity is possible. Lands where the surplus of product over labor is only middling suit free peoples. Those where the soil is abundant and fertile and gives a great product for little labor call for monarchical government, so that the surplus among the subjects can be consumed by the luxury of the prince; for it is better for this excess to be absorbed by the government than squandered among individuals. I am aware that there are exceptions; but the exceptions themselves confirm the rule, since sooner or later they produce revolutions that restore things to the natural order.

General laws should always be distinguished from the individual causes that may modify their effects. Even if all the South were covered with Republics and all the North with despotic States, it would still be true that, as far as climate goes, despotism suits hot countries, barbarism cold countries, and good polity temperate regions. I also see that, once the principle is granted, there may be disputes about applying it. It may be said that some cold countries are very fertile and some tropical countries very unproductive. But this difficulty exists only for those who do not consider the question in all its aspects. We must, as I have already said, take into account labor, strength, consumption and the rest.

Take two tracts of equal size, one yielding five and the other ten. If the inhabitants of the first consume four and those of the second nine, the surplus of the first will be a fifth and that of the second a tenth. The ratio of the two surpluses will then be the inverse of the ratio of the products, and the tract that produces only five will give a surplus twice that of the tract that produces ten.

But there is no question of a double product, and I think no one would, as a general rule, put the fertility of cold countries on a level with that of hot ones. Let us, however, suppose this equality. Let us, if you will, regard England as on the same level as Sicily, and Poland as Egypt — further south we shall have Africa and the Indies; further north, nothing at all. To get this equality of product, what a difference there must be in farming! In Sicily one need only scratch the ground; in England, how men must toil! But where more hands are needed to get the same product, the surplus must necessarily be smaller.

Consider, besides, that the same number of men consume much less in hot countries. The climate requires sobriety for the sake of health, and Europeans who try to live there as they would at home all die of dysentery and indigestion. “We are,” says Chardin, “carnivorous animals, wolves, compared with the Asiatics. Some attribute the sobriety of the Persians to their country being less cultivated; but I believe their country has fewer goods because the inhabitants need less. If their frugality,” he goes on, “were the effect of the barrenness of the land, only the poor would eat little; but everybody does. Again, people would eat less or more in different provinces, according to the land’s fertility; but the same sobriety is found throughout the kingdom. They are very proud of their way of life, saying that you have only to look at their complexion to see how far it excels that of the Christians. In fact, the Persians have an even complexion; their skins are fair, fine and smooth; while the complexion of their subjects the Armenians, who live in the European fashion, is rough and blotchy, and their bodies are gross and unwieldy.”

The nearer you get to the equator, the less people live on. They hardly touch meat; rice, maize, curcur, millet and cassava are their ordinary food. There are millions of men in the Indies whose subsistence does not cost a halfpenny a day. Even in Europe we find considerable differences of appetite between Northern and Southern peoples. A Spaniard will live for a week on a German’s dinner. In the countries where men are hungrier, luxury therefore turns toward consumption. In England luxury shows itself in a well-filled table; in Italy you feast on sugar and flowers.

Luxury in clothes shows similar differences. In climates where the seasons change quickly and violently, men have better and plainer clothes; where people dress only for show, what is striking matters more than what is useful, and clothes themselves are then a luxury. At Naples you may see men walking every day in the Pausilippeum in gold-embroidered upper garments and nothing else. It is the same with buildings: magnificence is the only concern where there is nothing to fear from the weather. In Paris and London you want to be lodged warmly and comfortably; in Madrid you have superb salons but not a window that closes, and you go to bed in a mere hole.
